d: RAG is a search engine wearing a language model as a hat. Trail compiles knowledge the way a brain consolidates memory — and the architectural difference shows up in latency, accuracy, provenance, and cost.
x: How Trail Works RAG does its work at query time on raw chunks; Trail does it at ingest time and stores the result as Neurons. Compiling costs more per source but less per query, and lets knowledge accumulate with provenance on every claim. This article is about the class of problems where it does not work — and about the architectural alternative Trail implements, which we describe as compile-time knowledge. The short version is this: RAG performs work at query time. Trail performs work at ingest time. That single difference cascades through every other property of the system — latency, accuracy, provenance, cost, accumulation, and the size of the corpus you can usefully reason over. We will walk through each of these. We will also explain why this distinction is not novel. Brains do compile-time knowledge work. They have done it for hundreds of millions of years. RAG, despite the surface-level analogy to memory retrieval, is structurally closer to a search engine than to a cognitive system. The reason this matters is practical: certain workloads accumulate value over time only if the system itself accumulates structure over time, and RAG does not. d: RAG treats knowledge like a filing cabinet. Brains do something fundamentally different — and so does trail. The architecture matters more than the model.

He read, he distilled, he filed — and the distilled material, threaded together by hand into a network of cards, became dense enough that querying it produced book-length output more or less by exposure. t: Scaling Trail from 200 to 100,000 Neurons: An Engineering Note
d: A compile-time knowledge engine has three workloads that fight for compute — ingest, lint, and the curation queue. Each one breaks at a different corpus size, for different reasons, and requires a different fix. This is the long-form companion to Work That Fits in a Night: the full accounting of where Trail's bottlenecks are, when they hit, and what a deployment looks like at 200, 8,000, 25,000, and 100,000 Neurons.
x: Research Ingest cost stays flat per source regardless of corpus size, so it never becomes the bottleneck. Contradiction lint hits a wall around 8,000 Neurons and is bounded by a capped pass of 500 Neurons from then on. From about 25,000 Neurons the limit is curator attention, met with auto-approval and roles, while infrastructure scales by bigger machines, not rewrites. scalability architecture lint ingest queue infrastructure sampling engineering-note llm-wiki karpathy Why this note exists · The three workloads · Ingest · Lint · Queue · 200 Neurons — the single-tenant zero-friction baseline · 8,000 Neurons — where the first wall lives · 25,000 Neurons — the second wall, and why it isn t about lint · 100,000 Neurons — the tier that rewrites the engine · Decision matrix — what to worry about, when · What breaks honestly · The through-line · See also Why this note exists Trail is a compile-time knowledge engine. Every source it ingests is read by a language model and turned into a persistent graph of Neurons — short wiki pages that cross-reference each other and the raw material they came from. The engine does three kinds of background work to keep that graph honest: it ingests new sources into Neurons, it lints the existing corpus for contradictions, orphans, and staleness, and it queues candidate edits for a human curator to approve. All three workloads scale differently. Ingest is largely linear in the size of the incoming source. Lint is quadratic if you let it be — each new Neuron wants to be re-checked against every existing peer. The queue is bounded by the number of decisions a human can make per day, which does not change no matter how large the corpus gets. At 200 Neurons none of this matters. A full lint pass finishes in twenty minutes. Ingest runs per-source without thinking about it. The queue holds a handful of candidates. Every shortcut in the engine falls inside a comfortable budget. At 100,000 Neurons the same code, run the same way, doesn t finish. The scheduler overlaps with itself. The LLM token spend outruns the pricing model. The curator drowns. The gap between works and doesn t work is not a cliff. It s a sequence of bottlenecks that arrive in a predictable order, each one requiring a distinct architectural response. The filters mirror NLP's deletion, generalisation and distortion and the brain's gating, and none is sufficient alone. curation nlp neuroscience architecture policy knowledge-engineering The gate is the architecture · What NLP actually said · The thalamic gate · Trail s three filters, one by one · Trusted pipeline — deletion by provenance · Confidence threshold — attention and arousal · No contradictions — cognitive dissonance · Why three and not one · The memex, again · Further reading The gate is the architecture Every persistent knowledge system eventually has to answer the same question: what gets written down, and on whose authority? For a brain, the answer is not conscious. You do not sit down each evening and decide which of the day s experiences to encode into long-term memory. Something in you decides, below the level of attention, and what gets through is the substrate of everything you will later think of as your understanding of the world. What gets filtered out is, by definition, unrecoverable — you will never know what you nearly remembered. For a knowledge infrastructure engine, the same question becomes an explicit design problem. Trail compiles sources into a cross-referenced graph of Neurons maintained by a language model. If every candidate that the compiler proposes were admitted without scrutiny, the graph would drift into incoherence within weeks. Contradictions would accumulate. Three filters on that gate, to be precise. They sit between the candidate queue and the Neurons themselves, and they decide — per candidate, per event — whether a piece of proposed knowledge gets auto-approved, gets raised to a human curator, or gets rejected outright. t: Work That Fits in a Night: How Trail Stops Caring About Corpus Size
d: A compile-time knowledge system has to integrate new sources against everything it already knows. That integration cost grows with the corpus — until, one Tuesday, it stops finishing before the next night begins. Here is how Trail makes that cost bounded without going blind to the long tail.
x: How Trail Works A full nightly contradiction scan stops fitting in a night at around 8,000 Neurons. Parallelising, skipping unchanged pages or uniform sampling all fail because contradictions mostly come from recent edits. Trail caps each pass at 500 Neurons, so queue size and cost stay flat however large the brain grows. scalability architecture sampling systems-design lint llm-wiki A graph that does not stop growing · The math of the wall · Why the obvious solutions are wrong · The split that works · What this looks like in a running system · The same pattern, used everywhere · What the user sees · The broader commitment · Further reading A graph that does not stop growing If you build a system that compiles knowledge at ingest time — as Trail does, and as Karpathy s LLM Wiki does, and as a brain does during sleep — you accept a particular kind of problem the moment the corpus crosses about eight thousand pages. Every new source wants to be integrated against everything the system already knows. Every existing page wants to be re-checked against every new claim. Contradictions should not accumulate silently. Stale references should surface. Orphaned Neurons — pages no source supports anymore — should get caught. All of this is correct, all of this is necessary, and all of this runs as a nightly background pass. The problem is that the nightly pass is not free, and at a certain corpus size it stops fitting inside the night. This is a post about that wall, how we hit it, and how we walked through it without the usual answers — without giving up on full-corpus consistency, without silently skipping old pages, and without turning the whole engine into a distributed computing project. x: The `[[...]]` double-bracket syntax that links one Neuron to another inside a Brain. The text between the brackets is slugified to resolve against a target filename — `[[Orphans + Stale]]` finds `orphans-stale.md`. Neuron-links build the graph that powers the Chat's context-gathering, the Backlink view in the reader, and the orphan-detector's "no one links here" signal. **How to author one:** type `[[Target Neuron Title]]` directly in any markdown content field — the Neuron editor, the "+ New" modal, a Work item's Description (Task / Bug / Milestone / Decision), or the save-dialog when you pin a Chat answer as a Neuron. The backlink extractor resolves it on save; the new edge appears in the Graph and the target Neuron's "N Neurons link here" count ticks up. The ingest pipeline also writes Neuron-links automatically when compiling Sources, so the Curator rarely has to add them by hand. Optional typed form `[[target|edge-type]]` carries a semantic relation — `cites` (default, bare mention), `is-a`, `part-of`, `contradicts`, `supersedes`, `example-of`, `caused-by` — and colours the graph accordingly. x: A URL- and filename-safe version of a title, produced by a deterministic transformation called *slugification*: lowercase everything, replace spaces with hyphens, strip punctuation, and fold non-ASCII characters to their closest ASCII equivalents (`æ→ae`, `ø→oe`, `å→aa`). Examples: `"Yin og Yang"` → `yin-og-yang`, `"Orphans + Stale"` → `orphans-stale`, `"Christian Broberg"` → `christian-broberg`. Slugs are the canonical address of a Neuron inside a Brain — the file is `<slug>.md`, the URL is `/kb/<kb-slug>/neurons/<slug>`, and a Neuron-link's `[[...]]` text gets slugified to find its target. Two different titles that slugify to the same string collide on the same Neuron, so the compiler avoids ambiguity by keeping titles distinctive in the source language. The Danish/English bilingual fold recognises that `yin-og-yang` and `yin-and-yang` should resolve to the same Neuron when the KB's language is Danish — protecting against LLM drift between `og` / `and`.

x: A Neuron-link that carries a named semantic relation, so the graph isn't just "A links to B" but "A *is-a* B" or "A *contradicts* B". Authored as `[[target|edge-type]]`. Seven recognised types: **cites** — bare mention, weakest relation, the default for every plain `[[link]]` and every older link; **is-a** — hierarchical specialisation (Labrador is-a Dog); **part-of** — composition (Keyboard part-of Laptop); **contradicts** — an explicit disagreement between two claims, feeds the contradiction-lint detector directly; **supersedes** — versioning (Constitution-1953 supersedes Constitution-1849); **example-of** — a concrete instance of an abstract concept (Pythagoras example-of Mathematician); **caused-by** — causal dependency (Flood caused-by Dam-break). The compile-prompt teaches the LLM when each type applies; the backlink extractor records the type in the DB on save; the Graph view colours edges by type with a legend-chip row, and the relationships API exposes a `?type=` filter for targeted queries ("show me everything this Neuron contradicts"). Turning a bare `[[link]]` into a typed one is a drop-in edit — no schema migration, the default stays `cites` for anything un-typed.

x: Full-Text Search — the keyword-based search engine indexed over every Neuron's content + title + tags. Trail uses SQLite's FTS5 module (built in, no external service). FTS powers (1) the search bar in admin, (2) chat's context-retrieval (which Neurons relate to this question?), (3) lint's peer-discovery (which Neurons might contradict this one?). FTS is keyword-fast, not semantic — it matches words, not meanings. Auto-syncs via DB triggers when Neurons are created/edited/archived, so the index is always fresh. On a Brain with hybrid search switched on, search and chat combine FTS with meaning-based matching (see Search).

d: The K best matches from a similarity search — the standard way to limit how many results a query returns. Trail uses top-K = 5 by default for contradiction-lint
x: The K best matches from a similarity search — the standard way to limit how many results a query returns. Trail uses top-K = 5 by default for contradiction-lint: when scanning a Neuron, take the 5 most-related peers (via FTS) and pair-compare. Higher K = better coverage but more LLM calls (cost grows linearly). Lower K = faster + cheaper but might miss contradictions hiding in less-obvious peers.

x: One knowledge base inside Trail — the Sources you add, the Neurons compiled from them, and the curator decisions that shaped them, held together by one topic or project. A tenant can have many Brains ("my reflexology Brain", "my iOS notes Brain"). Until September 2026 the admin called this unit "a Trail"; Trail is now the name of the product only.

x: Asking a Brain a question in plain language. Trail finds the Neurons that fit, writes an answer from them and shows which Neurons it used. Superseded Neurons and Neurons whose confidence has faded below 0.3 are left out, so old knowledge doesn't creep into new answers. A conversation can be saved as a Source, which compiles it back into the Brain.

x: Finding Neurons in a Brain. Every Brain has keyword search (FTS), and a Neuron whose title exactly matches your query is always ranked first. A Brain can additionally have hybrid search switched on, which also matches on meaning — so "opening hours" can find a Neuron that says "we're open from 9". Hybrid search is off by default and is turned on per Brain.

x: A short piece of a document — roughly 500 tokens, split along paragraphs and headings — that search indexes separately. Each chunk remembers which heading it sits under, so a search hit can point to the exact section instead of just the whole document.

x: A Neuron that holds a rule of thumb or a way of working ("always clarify the question before answering") rather than a fact. Its confidence drops the longer it goes unedited; below 0.3 it counts as faded and chat leaves it out, unless it is pinned. Heuristics are internal: external integrations never see them.

x: Each Neuron has a live confidence between 0 and 1, recalculated every night from how old it is, how many Sources back it, whether it is contradicted, and how often it is cited and read. Knowledge that is never used slowly weighs less in chat and search; it is never deleted. Fading is paused for a new Brain until you turn it on — so nothing fades before the site using the Brain is in real use. How fast each Neuron type fades can be adjusted on the Health page.

x: Marking a Neuron as always true. A pinned Neuron is held at full confidence (1.0) and never fades, so it always counts fully in chat and search. Use it for core facts and definitions that don't get old.

x: A Neuron that has been replaced by a newer one. It happens automatically when two Neurons contradict each other and one clearly wins — clearly higher confidence and at least as many Sources behind it — or when a new version of the same Source arrives. The old Neuron is kept for history, but chat no longer uses it and the graph tones it down. If neither side clearly wins, the contradiction goes to the Curator instead.

It replaces the old one instead of landing as a contradiction in the Queue. It is on by default and can be switched off for the whole Brain or per connector. If an upload only shares its name with an older file, mark it "This is a new source" so it replaces nothing.

x: A named point in a Brain's history that you can roll back to. Before a rollback you are shown exactly what will change, and Trail saves the current state as a version first, so the rollback itself can be undone.

x: A nightly check that measures, with numbers, whether a Brain's answers rest on its Sources and whether search finds the right Neuron. It is off by default, runs at most once a day per Brain and stops at a budget cap you set (75 cents a night by default). Results and findings appear at the top of the Health page.

x: A secret token that lets your own website, script or AI assistant talk to Trail — search, retrieve, chat or post knowledge. The full key is shown only once when you create it. x: Who is asking, which decides what they may see. Curator (you in the admin) sees everything.
